abstract: This study examines the origins and content of new work created in the U.S. labor market from 1940 to 2018. The authors find that while automation has increasingly eroded demand for labor across the past four decades, new work creation has fundamentally shifted away from production occupations toward high-paid professional roles, suggesting a structural transformation in the types of jobs emerging in response to technological change.
keyFindings: Demand-eroding effects of automation innovations have intensified over the past four decades
New work creation has shifted from production to high-paid professional occupations
The pattern of occupational change reflects a structural transformation in labor market dynamics between 1940 and 2018
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of U.S. labor market data from 1940–2018, examining occupational composition and work creation patterns across the full period.
